## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with diabetes based on statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Several of the strongest signals point to inflammation, tissue remodeling, vascular dysfunction, and endocrine intestinal biology as central features of diabetes. Notably, neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695, p = 2.95 × 10−19, associated proteins = 88), complement system (WP:WP2806, p = 1.01 × 10−7, associated proteins = 25), and viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (KEGG:04061, p = 1.20 × 10−12, associated proteins = 31) collectively indicate strong enrichment of innate immune and cytokine-linked pathways. This is consistent with extensive literature showing that chronic low-grade inflammation, activation of neutrophils, and complement-mediated injury contribute to insulin resistance, beta cell stress, and diabetic complications. In parallel, extracellular matrix organization (REAC:R-HSA-1474244, p = 4.90 × 10−14, associated proteins = 59), regulation of vasculature development (GO:1901342, p = 4.18 × 10−16, associated proteins = 50), lipid localization (GO:0010876, p = 2.83 × 10−11, associated proteins = 50), and atherosclerosis (HP:0002621, p = 4.10 × 10−2, associated proteins = 15) support the well-established link between diabetes, vascular injury, dyslipidemia, and extracellular matrix remodeling, which underlie microvascular and macrovascular disease. 

In addition, the strong enrichment of small intestine; endocrine cells[High] (HPA:0481293, p = 4.12 × 10−12, associated proteins = 51), duodenum; endocrine cells[≥Low] (HPA:0151291, p = 7.62 × 10−13, associated proteins = 74), microvillus (GO:0005902, p = 4.69 × 10−3, associated proteins = 10), and carbohydrate binding (GO:0030246, p = 3.04 × 10−15, associated proteins = 33) suggests involvement of intestinal nutrient sensing, absorptive surface biology, and enteroendocrine signaling, all of which are increasingly recognized as important regulators of glucose homeostasis and insulin secretion. Lysosome (KEGG:04142, p = 5.70 × 10−12, associated proteins = 35) and endopeptidase activity (GO:0004175, p = 3.04 × 10−15, associated proteins = 69) further point to altered proteolysis, autophagy-related degradation, and metabolic turnover, processes implicated in beta cell dysfunction and diabetic tissue injury. The enrichment of factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (TF:M10023_1, p = 1.79 × 10−2, associated proteins = 38) is also notable, as p53 has been linked in the literature to cellular stress responses, senescence, apoptosis, and metabolic dysregulation in diabetes. Finally, pathways such as axon (GO:0030424, p = 2.35 × 10−2, associated proteins = 29) and osteoarthritis (HP:0002758, p = 2.08 × 10−2, associated proteins = 14) may reflect complications and comorbid tissue damage, including diabetic neuropathy and degenerative joint changes. Overall, these highly significant enrichments support a model in which diabetes is driven not only by impaired glucose regulation, but also by coordinated immune activation, vascular remodeling, extracellular matrix changes, intestinal endocrine dysfunction, and stress-response signaling.
